chapter.title: Putting it all together: notes on the structure of Lojban texts

section.title: Introductory
section.para: This chapter is incurably miscellaneous. It describes the cmavo that specify the structure of Lojban texts, from the largest scale (paragraphs) to the smallest (single words). There are fewer examples than are found in other chapters of this book, since the linguistic mechanisms described are generally made use of in conversation or else in long documents.

This chapter is also not very self-contained. It makes passing reference to a great many concepts which are explained in full only in other chapters. The alternative would be a chapter on text structure which was as complex as all the other chapters put together. Lojban is a unified language, and it is not possible to understand any part of it (in full) before understanding every part of it (to some degree).

section.title: Sentences: I
section.para: The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

audio-visually isomorphic Since Lojban is audio-visually isomorphic, there needs to be a spoken and written way of signaling the end of a sentence and the start of the following one. In written English, a period serves this purpose; in spoken English, a tone contour (rising or falling) usually does the job, or sometimes a long pause. Lojban uses a single separator: the cmavo .i (of selma'o I):

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi klama le zarci .i do cadzu le bisli
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I go-to the store. - You walk-on the ice.

section.para:
sentencesseparator for joining
The word separator should be noted. .i is not normally used after the last sentence nor before the first one, although both positions are technically grammatical. .i signals a new sentence on the same topic, not necessarily by the same speaker. The relationship between the sentences is left vague, except in stories, where the relationship usually is temporal, and the following sentence states something that happened after the previous sentence.

Note that although the first letter of an English sentence is capitalized, the cmavo .i is never capitalized. In writing, it is appropriate to place extra space before .i to make it stand out better for the reader. In some styles of Lojban writing, every .i is placed at the beginning of a line, possibly leaving space at the end of the previous line.

An .i cmavo may or may not be used when the speaker of the following sentence is different from the speaker of the preceding sentence, depending on whether the sentences are felt to be connected or not.

An .i cmavo can be compounded with a logical or non-logical connective (a jek or joik), a modal or tense connective, or both: these constructs are explained in
,
, and . In all cases, the .i comes first in the compound. Attitudinals can also be attached to an .i if they are meant to apply to the whole sentence: see .

sentencesclose grouping
There exist a pair of mechanisms for binding a sequence of sentences closely together. If the .i (with or without connectives) is followed by bo (of selma'o BO), then the two sentences being separated are understood to be more closely grouped than sentences connected by .i alone.

titlespecifying with "tu'e…tu'u"
Similarly, a group of sentences can be preceded by tu'e (of selma'o TUhE) and followed by tu'u (of selma'o TUhU) to fuse them into a single unit. A common use of tu'e … tu'u is to group the sentences which compose a poem: the title sentence would precede the group, separated from it by .i. Another use might be a set of directions, where each numbered direction might be surrounded by tu'e … tu'u and contain one or more sentences separated by .i. Grouping with tu'e and tu'u is analogous to grouping with ke and ke'e to establish the scope of logical or non-logical connectives (see ).

section.title: Paragraphs: NIhO
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

The paragraph is a concept used in writing systems for two purposes: to indicate changes of topic, and to break up the hard-to-read appearance of large blocks of text on the page. The former function is represented in both spoken and written Lojban by the cmavo ni'o and no'i , both of selma'o NIhO. Of these two, ni'o is the more common. By convention, written Lojban is broken into paragraphs just before any ni'o or no'i , but a very long passage on a single topic might be paragraphed before an .i. On the other hand, it is conventional in English to start a new paragraph in dialogue when a new speaker starts, but this convention is not commonly observed in Lojban dialogues. Of course, none of these conventions affect meaning in any way.

paragraphsseparator
old topic A ni'o can take the place of an .i as a sentence separator, and in addition signals a new topic or paragraph. Grammatically, any number of ni'o cmavo can appear consecutively and are equivalent to a single one; semantically, a greater number of ni'o cmavo indicates a larger-scale change of topic. This feature allows complexly structured text, with topics, subtopics, and sub-subtopics, to be represented clearly and unambiguously in both spoken and written Lojban. However, some conventional differences do exist between ni'o in writing and in conversation.

paragraph separationwritten text
tensescope effect of new paragraph
indicatorsscope effect of new paragraph
pro-sumtiscope effect of new paragraph
pro-bridiscope effect of new paragraph
paragraphseffects on scope
discursive indicator indicator scope In written text, a single ni'o is a mere discursive indicator of a new subject, whereas ni'oni'o marks a change in the context. In this situation, ni'oni'o implicitly cancels the definitions of all pro-sumti of selma'o KOhA as well as pro-bridi of selma'o GOhA. (Explicit cancelling is expressed by the cmavo da'o of selma'o DAhO, which has the free grammar of an indicator – it can appear almost anywhere.) The use of ni'oni'o does not affect indicators (of selma'o UI) or tense references, but ni'oni'oni'o , indicating a drastic change of topic, would serve to reset both indicators and tenses. (See
for a discussion of indicator scope.)

paragraph separationspoken text
Arabian Nights In spoken text, which is inherently less structured, these levels are reduced by one, with ni'o indicating a change in context sufficient to cancel pro-sumti and pro-bridi assignment. On the other hand, in a book, or in stories within stories such as The Arabian Nights , further levels may be expressed by extending the ni'o string as needed. Normally, a written text will begin with the number of ni'o cmavo needed to signal the largest scale division which the text contains. ni'o strings may be subscripted to label each context of discourse: see .

previous topic no'i is similar in effect to ni'o , but indicates the resumption of a previous topic. In speech, it is analogous to (but much shorter than) such English discursive phrases as But getting back to the point .... By default, the topic resumed is that in effect before the last ni'o. When subtopics are nested within topics, then no'i would resume the previous subtopic and no'ino'i the previous topic. Note that no'i also resumes tense and pro-sumti assignments dropped at the previous ni'o.

subscripted topics If a ni'o is subscripted, then a no'i with the same subscript is assumed to be a continuation of it. A no'i may also have a negative subscript, which would specify counting backwards a number of paragraphs and resuming the topic found thereby.

section.title: Topic-comment sentences: ZOhU
section.para: The following cmavo is discussed in this section:
The normal Lojban sentence is just a bridi, parallel to the normal English sentence which has a subject and a predicate:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I went-to the market

section.para:
topic-commentdescription
In Chinese, the normal sentence form is different: a topic is stated, and a comment about it is made. (Japanese also has the concept of a topic, but indicates it by attaching a suffix; other languages also distinguish topics in various ways.) The topic says what the sentence is about:

listitem.para: 这消息我知道了。
Zhè xiāoxī wǒ zhīdàole.
this news : I know [perfective]
As for this news, I knew it.
I've heard this news already.

section.para:
The colon in the first two versions of
separate the topic ( this news) from the comment ( I know already).
Lojban uses the cmavo zo'u (of selma'o ZOhU) to separate topic (a sumti) from comment (a bridi):

interlinear-gloss.jbo: le nuzba zo'u mi co'i facki

section.para: is the literal Lojban translation of . Of course, the topic-comment structure can be changed to a straightforward bridi structure:

means the same as
, and it is simpler. However, often the position of the topic in the place structure of the selbri within the comment is vague:

Is the fish eating or being eaten? The sentence doesn't say. The Chinese equivalent of
is:

listitem.para: 鱼吃
yú chī
fish: eat

section.para: which is vague in exactly the same way.

Grammatically, it is possible to have more than one sumti before zo'u. This is not normally useful in topic-comment sentences, but is necessary in the other use of zo'u : to separate a quantifying section from a bridi containing quantified variables. This usage belongs to a discussion of quantifier logic in Lojban (see ), but an example would be:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: su'o de zo'u de patfu da
interlinear-gloss.gloss: there-exists-a Y such-that Y is-the-father-of X.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Every person has a father.

section.para: The string of sumti before zo'u (called the prenex : see ) may contain both a topic and bound variables:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: loi patfu ro da poi prenu ku'o
interlinear-gloss.gloss: As-for fathers: for-all X which are-persons, -

interlinear-gloss.jbo: … su'o de zo'u de patfu da
interlinear-gloss.gloss: … there-exists-a Y such-that Y is-the-father-of X.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: As for fathers, every person has one.

section.para:
topic/commentmultiple sentence
To specify a topic which affects more than one sentence, wrap the sentences in tu'e … tu'u brackets and place the topic and the zo'u directly in front. This is the exception to the rule that a topic attaches directly to a sentence:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: loi jdini zo'u tu'e - do ponse .inaja do djica [tu'u]
interlinear-gloss.gloss: Money : ( [if] you possess, then you want )
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Money: if you have it, you want it.

section.para:
Note: In Lojban, you do not want money ; you want to have money or something of the sort, as the x2 place of djica demands an event. As a result, the straightforward rendering of
without a topic is not:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: do ponse loi--jdini .inaja do djica ri
interlinear-gloss.gloss: You possess money only-if you desire it.

section.para: where ri repeats loi jdini , a group of money. But djica requires an event in that place, not a thing, so say instead:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: do ponse loi--jdini .inaja do djica tu'a ri
interlinear-gloss.gloss: You possess money only-if you desire something-about it.

section.para:
namely, the possession of money. But topic-comment sentences like
are inherently vague, and this difference between ponse (which expects a physical object in x2) and djica is ignored. See
for another topic/comment sentence.

The subject of an English sentence is often the topic as well, but in Lojban the sumti in the x1 place is not necessarily the topic, especially if it is the normal (unconverted) x1 for the selbri. Thus Lojban sentences don't necessarily have a subject in the English sense.

section.title: Questions and answers
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

questionstruth
Lojban questions are not at all like English questions. There are two basic types: truth questions, of the form Is it true that ... , and fill-in-the-blank questions. Truth questions are marked by preceding the bridi, or following any part of it specifically questioned, with the cmavo xu (of selma'o UI):

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Are you going to the store/Did you go to the store?

section.para: (Since the Lojban is tenseless, either colloquial translation might be correct.) Truth questions are further discussed in .

questionsfill-in-the-blank
Fill-in-the-blank questions have a cmavo representing some Lojban word or phrase which is not known to the questioner, and which the answerer is to supply. There are a variety of cmavo belonging to different selma'o which provide different kinds of blanks.

questionssumti
Where a sumti is not known, a question may be formed with ma (of selma'o KOhA), which is a kind of pro-sumti:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Who is going to the store?

section.para: Of course, the ma need not be in the x1 place:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Where are you going?

section.para: The answer is a simple sumti:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: The store.

section.para: A sumti, then, is a legal utterance, although it does not by itself constitute a bridi – it does not claim anything, but merely completes the open-ended claim of the previous bridi.

questionsmultiple
There can be two ma cmavo in a single question:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Who goes where?

section.para: and the answer would be two sumti, which are meant to fill in the two ma cmavo in order:
An even more complex example, depending on the non-logical connective fa'u (of selma'o JOI), which is like the English and ... respectively :

interlinear-gloss.jbo: ma fa'u ma klama ma fa'u ma
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Who and who goes where and where, -respectively?

section.para: An answer might be

interlinear-gloss.jbo: la .djan. la .marcas. le zarci le briju
interlinear-gloss.gloss: - John, - Marsha, the store, the office.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: John and Marsha go to the store and the office, respectively.

section.para:
(Note: A mechanical substitution of
into
produces an ungrammatical result, because * ... le zarci fa'u le briju is ungrammatical Lojban: the first le zarci has to be closed with its proper terminator ku , for reasons explained in . This effect is not important: Lojban behaves as if all elided terminators have been supplied in both question and answer before inserting the latter into the former. The exchange is grammatical if question and answer are each separately grammatical.)

questionsselbri
Questions to be answered with a selbri are expressed with mo of selma'o GOhA, which is a kind of pro-bridi:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: What is Lojban?

section.para: predicate answers Here the answerer is to supply some predicate which is true of Lojban. Such questions are extremely open-ended, due to the enormous range of possible predicate answers. The answer might be just a selbri, or might be a full bridi, in which case the sumti in the answer override those provided by the questioner. To limit the range of a mo question, make it part of a tanru.

questionsnumber
Questions about numbers are expressed with xo of selma'o PA:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: How many people did you see?

section.para: The answer would be a simple number, another kind of non-bridi utterance:

Fill-in-the-blank questions may also be asked about: logical connectives (using cmavo ji of A, ge'i of GA, gi'i of GIhA, gu'i of GUhA, or je'i of JA, and receiving an ek, gihek, ijek, or ijoik as an answer) – see
; attitudes (using pei of UI, and receiving an attitudinal as an answer) – see
; place structures (using fi'a of FA, and receiving a cmavo of FA as an answer) – see
; tenses and modals (using cu'e of CUhE, and receiving any tense or BAI cmavo as an answer) – see
and .

Questions can be marked by placing pau (of selma'o UI) before the question bridi. See
for details.
The full list of non-bridi utterances suitable as answers to questions is:

listitem.para:
linked arguments utterancesnon-bridi
any number of sumti (with elidable terminator vau , see )
an ek or gihek (logical connectives, see )
a number, or any mathematical expression placed in parentheses (see )
a bare na negator (to negate some previously expressed bridi), or corresponding ja'a affirmer (see )
a relative clause (to modify some previously expressed sumti, see )
a prenex/topic (to modify some previously expressed bridi, see )
linked arguments (beginning with be or bei and attached to some previously expressed selbri, often in a description, see )

section.para: At the beginning of a text, the following non-bridi are also permitted:

listitem.para: one or more cmevla (to indicate direct address without doi , see )
indicators (to express a prevailing attitude, see )

section.para: Where not needed for the expression of answers, most of these are made grammatical for pragmatic reasons: people will say them in conversation, and there is no reason to rule them out as ungrammatical merely because most of them are vague.

section.title: Subscripts: XI
section.para: The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

subscripting The cmavo xi (of selma'o XI) indicates that a subscript (a number, a lerfu string, or a parenthesized mekso) follows. Subscripts can be attached to almost any construction and are placed following the construction (or its terminator word, which is generally required). When attached to cmavo they are useful either to extend the finite cmavo list to infinite length, or to make more refined distinctions than the standard cmavo list permits. The remainder of this section mentions some places where subscripts might naturally be used.
Lojban gismu have at most five places:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi cu klama - le zarci -- le zdani -- le dargu -- le karce
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I -- go to the market from the house via the road using the car.

section.para:
Consequently, selma'o SE (which operates on a selbri to change the order of its places) and selma'o FA (which provides place number tags for individual sumti) have only enough members to handle up to five places. Conversion of
, using xe to swap the x1 and x5 places, would produce:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: le karce cu xe-klama - le zarci
interlinear-gloss.gloss: The car -- is-a-transportation-means to the market
… from the house via the road for me.

section.para: And reordering of the place structures might produce:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: fo le dargu fi le zdani fa mi
interlinear-gloss.gloss: Via the road, from the house, - I,

interlinear-gloss.jbo: … fe le zarci fu le karce cu klama
interlinear-gloss.gloss: … to the market, using the car, - go.

section.para:
to
all mean the same thing. But consider the lujvo nunkla , formed by applying the abstraction operator nu to klama :

interlinear-gloss.jbo: … - le zarci -- le zdani -- le dargu -- le karce
interlinear-gloss.gloss: … to the market from the house via the road using the car.

section.para:
SE selma'oafter 5th place
se FA selma'oafter 5th place
SE selma'oafter 5th place
subscriptsand sumti re-ordering
shows that nunkla has six places: the five places of klama plus a new one (placed first) for the event itself. Performing transformations similar to that of
requires an additional conversion cmavo that exchanges the x1 and x6 places. The solution is to use any cmavo of SE with a subscript "6" ( ):

interlinear-gloss.gloss: … to the market from the house

section.para: Likewise, a sixth place tag can be created by using any cmavo of FA with a subscript:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: fu le dargu fo le zdani fe mi
interlinear-gloss.gloss: Via the road, from the house, by me,

interlinear-gloss.jbo: … fi le zarci faxixa le karce cu nunkla
interlinear-gloss.gloss: … to the market, using the car, - is-an-event-of-going.

section.para:
to
also all mean the same thing, and each is derived straightforwardly from any of the others, despite the tortured nature of the English glosses. In addition, any other member of SE or FA could be substituted into sexixa and faxixa without change of meaning: vexixa means the same thing as sexixa.

ko'a-seriesafter tenth
da-seriesafter third
subscriptsand pro-sumti
Lojban provides two groups of pro-sumti, both belonging to selma'o KOhA. The ko'a-series cmavo are used to refer to explicitly specified sumti to which they have been bound using goi. The da-series, on the other hand, are existentially or universally quantified variables. (These concepts are explained more fully in .) There are ten ko'a-series cmavo and 3 da-series cmavo available.

da da-seriesmore than three variables under one scope
ko'a-seriesmore than three variables under one scope
If more are required, any cmavo of the ko'a-series or the da-series can be subscripted:
is the 4th bound variable of the 1st sequence of the da-series, and

is the 19th free variable of the 3rd sequence of the ko'a-series. This convention allows 10 sequences of ko'a-type pro-sumti and 3 sequences of da-type pro-sumti, each with as many members as needed. Note that daxivo and dexivo are considered to be distinct pro-sumti, unlike the situation with sexixa and vexixa above. Exactly similar treatment can be given to the bu'a-series of selma'o GOhA and to the gismu pro-bridi broda , brode , brodi , brodo , and brodu.

subscriptsmathematical
Subscripts on lerfu words are used in the standard mathematical way to extend the number of variables:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: li xy.boixipa du li xy.boixire su'i xy.boixici
interlinear-gloss.gloss: The-number x-sub-1 equals the-number x-sub-2 plus x-sub-3

section.para:
and can be used to extend the number of pro-sumti as well, since lerfu strings outside mathematical contexts are grammatically and semantically equivalent to pro-sumti of the ko'a-series. (In
, note the required terminator boi after each xy. cmavo; this terminator allows the subscript to be attached without ambiguity.)

subscriptsand names
Names, which are similar to pro-sumti, can also be subscripted to distinguish two individuals with the same name:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: la .djan. xipa cusku lu mi'enai do li'u la .djan. xire
interlinear-gloss.gloss: - John 1 expresses [quote] I-am-not you [unquote] to - John 2.

section.para:
subscriptsand tense
Subscripts on tenses allow talking about more than one time or place that is described by the same general cmavo. For example, puxipa could refer to one point in the past, and puxire a second point (earlier or later).

subscriptsand fuzzy truths
You can place a subscript on the word ja'a , the bridi affirmative of selma'o NA, to express so-called fuzzy truths. The usual machinery for fuzzy logic (statements whose truth value is not merely true or false , but is expressed by a number in the range 0 to 1) in Lojban is the abstractor jei :
However, by convention we can attach a subscript to ja'a to indicate fuzzy truth (or to na if we change the amount):

subscriptsand paragraph separators
Finally, as mentioned in
, ni'o and no'i cmavo with matching subscripts mark the start and the continuation of a given topic respectively. Different topics can be assigned to different subscripts.
Other uses of subscripts will doubtless be devised in future.

section.title: Utterance ordinals: MAI
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
Numerical free modifiers, corresponding to English firstly , secondly , and so on, can be created by suffixing mai or mo'o of selma'o MAI to a number or a lerfu string. Here are some examples:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi klama pamai le zarci .e remai le zdani
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I go-to (firstly) the store and (secondly) the house.

section.para: This does not imply that I go to the store before I go to the house: that meaning requires a tense. The sumti are simply numbered for convenience of reference. Like other free modifiers, the utterance ordinals can be inserted almost anywhere in a sentence without affecting its grammar or its meaning.

Any of the Lojban numbers can be used with MAI: romai , for example, means all-thly or lastly. Likewise, if you are enumerating a long list and have forgotten which number is wanted next, you can say ny.mai , or Nthly.

The difference between mai and mo'o is that mo'o enumerates larger subdivisions of a text; mai was designed for lists of numbered items, whereas mo'o was intended to subdivide structured works. If this chapter were translated into Lojban, it might number each section with mo'o : this section would then be introduced with zemo'o , or Section 7.

section.title: Attitude scope markers: FUhE/FUhO
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

UI selma'oscope of
Lojban has a complex system of attitudinals , words which indicate the speaker's attitude to what is being said. The attitudinals include indicators of emotion, intensity markers, discursives (which show the structure of discourse), and evidentials (which indicate how the speaker knows). Most of these words belong to selma'o UI; the intensity markers belong to selma'o CAI for historical reasons, but the two selma'o are grammatically identical. The individual cmavo of UI and CAI are discussed in
; only the rules for applying them in discourse are presented here.

Normally, an attitudinal applies to the preceding word only. However, if the preceding word is a structural cmavo which begins or ends a whole construction, then that whole construction is affected by the attitudinal:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I see the house, which I believe to be blue.
I see the blue thing, which I believe to be a house.
I see what I believe to be a blue house.

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi viska le blanu zdani ku .ia
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I see what I believe to be a blue house.

section.para: An attitudinal meant to cover a whole sentence can be attached to the preceding .i , expressed or understood:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I believe I see a blue house.

section.para: or to an explicit vau placed at the end of a bridi.
Likewise, an attitudinal meant to cover a whole paragraph can be attached to ni'o or no'i. An attitudinal at the beginning of a text applies to the whole text.

However, sometimes it is necessary to be more specific about the range of one or more attitudinals, particularly if the range crosses the boundaries of standard Lojban syntactic constructions. The cmavo fu'e (of selma'o FUhE) and fu'o (of selma'o FUhO) provide explicit scope markers. Placing fu'e in front of an attitudinal disconnects it from what precedes it, and instead says that it applies to all following words until further notice. The notice is given by fu'o , which can appear anywhere and cancels all in-force attitudinals. For example:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi viska le fu'e .ia blanu zdani fu'o ponse
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I see the [start] [belief] blue house [end] possessor
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I see the owner of what I believe to be a blue house.

section.para: Here, only the blanu zdani portion of the three-part tanru blanu zdani ponse is marked as a belief of the speaker. Naturally, the attitudinal scope markers do not affect the rules for interpreting multi-part tanru: blanu zdani groups first because tanru group from left to right unless overridden with ke or bo.
Other attitudinals of more local scope can appear after attitudinals marked by FUhE; these attitudinals are added to the globally active attitudinals rather than superseding them.

section.title: Quotations: LU, LIhU, LOhU, LEhU
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
Grammatically, quotations are very simple in Lojban: all of them are sumti, and they all mean something like the piece of text here quoted :

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I said, I'm John.

section.para: But in fact there are four different flavors of quotation in the language, involving six cmavo of six different selma'o. This being the case, quotation deserves some elaboration.

The simplest kind of quotation, exhibited in
, uses the cmavo lu (of selma'o LU) as the opening quotation mark, and the cmavo li'u (of selma'o LIhU) as the closing quotation mark. The text between lu and li'u must be a valid, parseable Lojban text. If the quotation is ungrammatical, so is the surrounding expression. The cmavo li'u is technically an elidable terminator, but it's almost never possible to elide it except at the end of text.

The cmavo lo'u (of selma'o LOhU) and le'u (of selma'o LEhU) are used to surround a quotation that is not necessarily grammatical Lojban. However, the text must consist of morphologically correct Lojban words (as defined in ), so that the le'u can be picked out reliably. The words need not be meaningful, but they must be recognizable as cmavo, brivla, or cmevla. Quotation with lo'u is essential to quoting ungrammatical Lojban for teaching in the language, the equivalent of the * that is used in English to mark such errors:
is grammatical even though the embedded quotation is not. Similarly, lo'u quotation can quote fragments of a text which themselves do not constitute grammatical utterances:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: In the sentence le mlatu cu viska le finpe , viska le should be replaced by viska lo.

section.para: Note the topic-comment formulation ( ) and the indicator applying to the selbri only ( ). Neither viska le nor viska lo is a valid Lojban utterance, and both require lo'u quotation.
Additionally, pro-sumti or pro-bridi in the quoting sentence can refer to words appearing in the quoted sentence when lu … li'u is used, but not when lo'u ... le'u is used:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: la .tcarlis. cusku lu le ninmu cu morsi li'u

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Charlie says The woman is dead , but she is alive.

section.para:
In
, ri is a pro-sumti which refers to the most recent previous sumti, namely le ninmu. Compare:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: la .tcarlis. cusku lo'u le ninmu cu morsi le'u
interlinear-gloss.gloss: - Charlie says [quote] le ninmu cu morsi [unquote].

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Charlie says le ninmu cu morsi , but he is alive.

section.para:
In
, ri cannot refer to the referent of the alleged sumti le ninmu , because le ninmu cu morsi is a mere uninterpreted sequence of Lojban words. Instead, ri ends up referring to the referent of the sumti la .tcarlis. , and so it is Charlie who is alive.

The metalinguistic erasers si , sa , and su , discussed in
, do not operate in text between lo'u and le'u. Indeed, nothing operates inside a lo'u…le'u quotation: the very first le'u encountered ends it, unconditionally – there is no way to smuggle a le'u inside, not even with zo (the first edition said otherwise; the rule was settled the simple way). It follows that lo'u…le'u quotations cannot nest; nor can a closed quotation be reopened – to add more quoted words, join a second quotation to it with joi. To quote text that itself contains le'u , use zoi (). Note that le'u is not an elidable terminator; it is required.

lo'urules, status of
(A status note: the lo'u…le'u rules of this section – the unconditional first le'u , no nesting, no reopening – are checkpointed: they follow the committee's frozen 2005 quotations decision, which replaced the first edition's zo le'u loophole.)

section.title: More on quotations: ZO, ZOI
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

The cmavo zo (of selma'o ZO) is a strong quotation mark for the single following word, which can be any Lojban word whatsoever – with one curious exception: the hesitation noise .y. is invisible to the word-level machinery, so zo skips right over it and quotes the word after it instead (see ). Among other uses, zo allows a metalinguistic word to be referenced without having it act on the surrounding text. The word must be a morphologically legal (but not necessarily meaningful) single Lojban word; compound cmavo are not permitted. For example:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: si is a Lojbanic word.

section.para: Since zo acts on a single word only, there is no corresponding terminator. Brevity, then, is a great advantage of zo , since the terminators for other kinds of quotation are rarely or never elidable.

The cmavo zoi (of selma'o ZOI) is a quotation mark for quoting non-Lojban text. Its syntax is zoi .X. text .X , where X is a single Lojban word (called the delimiting word) which is separated from the quoted text by pauses, and which is not found in the written text or spoken phoneme stream. Both occurrences of the delimiting word are required – neither may be elided – and within this construct the delimiting word serves purely as a bracket, losing whatever grammatical function it has elsewhere. It is common, but not required, to use the lerfu word (of selma'o BY) which corresponds to the Lojban name of the language being quoted:

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: zoi gy. John is a man .gy. cu glico jufra
interlinear-gloss.natlang: John is a man is an English sentence.

section.para: where gy. stands for glico. Other popular choices of delimiting words are .kuot. , a cmevla which sounds like the English word quote , and the word zoi itself. Another possibility is a Lojban word suggesting the topic of the quotation.

Within written text, the Lojban written word used as a delimiting word may not appear, whereas within spoken text, the sound of the delimiting word may not be uttered. This leads to occasional breakdowns of audio-visual isomorphism:
is fine in speech but ungrammatical as written, whereas
is correct when written but ungrammatical in speech.

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: mi djuno fi le valsi po'u zoi gy. gyrations .gy.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I know about the word which-is gyrations.

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: mi djuno fi le valsi po'u zoi jai. gyrations .jai
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I know about the word which-is gyrations.

section.para: The text gy. appears in the written word gyrations , whereas the sound represented in Lojban by jai appears in the spoken word gyrations. Such borderline cases should be avoided as a matter of good style.

It should be noted particularly that zoi quotation is the only way to quote rafsi, specifically CCV rafsi, because they are not Lojban words, and zoi quotation is the only way to quote things which are not Lojban words. (CVC and CVV rafsi look like cmevla and cmavo respectively, and so can be quoted using other methods.) For example:

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: zoi ry. sku .ry. cu rafsi zo cusku
interlinear-gloss.natlang:
sku
is a rafsi of
cusku .

section.para: (A minor note on interaction between lo'u ... le'u and zoi : inside a lo'u…le'u quotation, zoi is just another quoted word – it does not begin a quotation there, and the material between lo'u and le'u must accordingly consist entirely of Lojban words. Conversely, a zoi quotation elsewhere may of course mention le'u safely, since zoi captures everything up to its delimiting word.)
Lojban strictly avoids any confusion between things and the names of things:

In
, zo .bab. is the word, whereas la .bab. is the thing named by the word. The cmavo la'e and lu'e (of selma'o LAhE) convert back and forth between references and their referents:

interlinear-gloss.gloss: The-word Bob is-the-name-of the-referent-of the-word Bob.

section.para:
through
all mean approximately the same thing, except for differences in emphasis.
is different:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Bob is the name of Bob.

section.para: and says that Bob is both the name and the thing named, an unlikely situation. People are not names.

(In
through
, the name .bab. was separated from a preceding zo by a pause, thus: zo .bab.. The reason for this extra pause is that all Lojban names must be separated by pause from any preceding word. There are numerous other cmavo that may precede a name: of these, zo is one of the most common.)

The cmavo la'o also belongs to selma'o ZOI, and is mentioned here for completeness, although it does not signal the beginning of a quotation. Instead, la'o serves to mark non-Lojban names, especially the Linnaean binomial names (such as Homo sapiens) which are the internationally standardized names for species of animals and plants. Internationally known names which can more easily be recognized by spelling rather than pronunciation, such as Goethe , can also appear in Lojban text with la'o :

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: la'o dy. Goethe .dy. cu me la'o ly. Homo sapiens .ly.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Goethe is a Homo sapiens.

section.para:
Using la'o for all names rather than Lojbanizing, however, makes for very cumbersome text. A rough equivalent of la'o might be la me zoi : here me turns the zoi quotation into a selbri meaning is among the referents of the quoted thing , and la builds a name from that selbri (see
for me).

zoidelimiter rules, status of
(A status note: the zoi and la'o delimiter rules of this section – any single Lojban word as delimiter, the payload running to the delimiter's next occurrence, the functionless bracket words, the required closing delimiter – are checkpointed: they follow the committee's frozen 2005 quotations decision, as does the zo rule of the previous section.)

section.title: Contrastive emphasis: BAhE
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
English often uses strong stress on a word to single it out for contrastive emphasis, thus
is quite different from

The heavy stress on
George
(represented in writing by italics) indicates that I saw George rather than someone else. Lojban does not use stress in this way: stress is used only to help separate words (because every brivla is stressed on the penultimate syllable) and in names to match other languages' stress patterns. Note that many other languages do not use stress in this way either; typically word order is rearranged, producing something like

example.para: It was George whom I saw.

section.para: In Lojban, the cmavo ba'e (of selma'o BAhE) precedes a single word which is to be emphasized:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I saw George.

section.para: Note the pause before the cmevla djordj. , which serves to separate it unambiguously from the ba'e. Alternatively, the ba'e can be moved to a position before the la , which in effect emphasizes the whole construct la .djordj. :

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I saw George.

section.para: Marking a word with a cmavo of BAhE does not change the word's grammar in any way. Any word in a bridi can receive contrastive emphasis marking:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I, no one else, saw George.
I saw (not heard or smelled) George.

section.para: Emphasis on one of the structural components of a Lojban bridi can also be achieved by rearranging it into an order that is not the speaker's or writer's usual order. Any sumti moved out of place, or the selbri when moved out of place, is emphatic to some degree.
For completeness, the cmavo za'e should be mentioned, also of selma'o BAhE. It marks a word as possibly irregular, non-standard, or nonce (created for the occasion):
marks a Lojbanization of an English name, where a more appropriate standard form might be something like la .ckiipyris. , reflecting the country's name in Albanian.

unabridged dictionary Before a lujvo or fu'ivla, za'e indicates that the word has been made up on the spot and may be used in a sense that is not found in the unabridged dictionary (when we have an unabridged dictionary!).

section.title: Parenthesis and metalinguistic commentary: TO, TOI, SEI
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

The cmavo to and toi are discursive (non-mathematical) parentheses, for inserting parenthetical remarks. Any text whatsoever can go within the parentheses, and it is completely invisible to its context. It can, however, refer to the context by the use of pro-sumti and pro-bridi: any that have been assigned in the context are still assigned in the parenthetical remarks, but the reverse is not true.

interlinear-gloss.jbo: doi .lisas. mi djica le nu to doi .frank.
interlinear-gloss.gloss: O Lisa, I desire the event-of ( O Frank,

interlinear-gloss.jbo: … ko sisti toi do viska le mlatu
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Lisa, I want you to (Frank! Stop!) see the cat.

section.para: implicitly redefines do within the parentheses: the listener is changed by doi .frank. When the context sentence resumes, however, the old listener, Lisa, is automatically restored.

editorial commentary There is another cmavo of selma'o TO: to'i. The difference between to and to'i is the difference between parentheses and square brackets in English prose. Remarks within to ... toi cmavo are implicitly by the same speaker, whereas remarks within to'i ... toi are implicitly by someone else, perhaps an editor:

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: la .frank. cusku lu mi prami do to'isa'a do du la .djein. toi li'u
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Frank expresses I love you [you = Jane]

section.para: editorial insertion bracketed remark The sa'a suffix is a discursive cmavo (of selma'o UI) meaning editorial insertion , and indicating that the marked word or construct (in this case, the entire bracketed remark) is not part of the quotation. It is required whenever the to'i ... toi remark is physically within quotation marks, at least when speaking to literal-minded listeners; the convention may be relaxed if no actual confusion results.

Note: The parser believes that parentheses are attached to the previous word or construct, because it treats them as syntactic equivalents of subscripts and other such so-called free modifiers. Semantically, however, parenthetical remarks are not necessarily attached either to what precedes them or what follows them.

metalinguistic commentwith embedded discursive
discursivesembedded
embedded discursive The cmavo sei (of selma'o SEI) begins an embedded discursive bridi. Comments added with sei are called metalinguistic , because they are comments about the discourse itself rather than about the subject matter of the discourse. This sense of the term metalinguistic is used throughout this chapter, and is not to be confused with the sense language for expressing other languages.
When marked with sei , a metalinguistic utterance can be embedded in another utterance as a discursive. In this way, discursives which do not have cmavo assigned in selma'o UI can be expressed:

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: la .frank. prami sei la .frank. gleki la .djein.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Frank loves (Frank is happy) Jane.

section.para: Using the happiness attitudinal, .ui , would imply that the speaker was happy. Instead, the speaker attributes happiness to Frank. It would probably be safe to elide the one who is happy, and say:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Frank loves (he is happy) Jane.

section.para: The grammar of the bridi following sei has an unusual limitation: the sumti must either precede the selbri, or must be glued into the selbri with be and bei :

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: la .frank. prami sei gleki be fa la .suzn. la .djein.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Frank loves (Susan is happy) Jane.

section.para: This restriction allows the terminator cmavo se'u to almost always be elided.

referenceand discursive utterances
pro-sumtiand discursive utterances
metalinguistic levels or reference metalinguistic levels Since a discursive utterance is working at a higher level of abstraction than a non-discursive utterance, a non-discursive utterance cannot refer to a discursive utterance. Specifically, the various back-counting, reciprocal, and reflexive constructs in selma'o KOhA ignore the utterances at higher metalinguistic levels in determining their referent. It is possible, and sometimes necessary, to refer to lower metalinguistic levels. For example, the English he said in a conversation is metalinguistic. For this purpose, quotations are considered to be at a lower metalinguistic level than the surrounding context (a quoted text cannot refer to the statements of the one who quotes it), whereas parenthetical remarks are considered to be at a higher level than the context.
Lojban works differently from English in that the he said can be marked instead of the quotation. In Lojban, you can say:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: la .djan. cusku lu mi klama le zarci li'u
interlinear-gloss.gloss: - John expresses [quote] I go-to the store [unquote].

section.para: which literally claims that John uttered the quoted text. If the central claim is that John made the utterance, as is likely in conversation, this style is the most sensible. However, in written text which quotes a conversation, you don't want the he said or she said to be considered part of the conversation. If unmarked, it could mess up the anaphora counting. Instead, you can use:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: lu mi klama le zarci seisa'a

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I go to the store , said John.

section.para: And of course other orders are possible:

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: lu seisa'a la .djan. cusku be dei mi klama le zarci
interlinear-gloss.natlang: John said, I go to the store.

interlinear-gloss.jbophrase: lu mi klama seisa'a la djan cusku le zarci
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I go , John said, to the store.

section.para: Note the sa'a following each sei , marking the sei and its attached bridi as an editorial insert, not part of the quotation. In a more relaxed style, these sa'a cmavo would probably be dropped.

The elidable terminator for sei is se'u (of selma'o SEhU); it is rarely needed, except to separate a selbri within the sei comment from an immediately following selbri (or component) outside the comment.

section.title: Erasure: SI, SA, SU
section.para: The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

erasureword
The cmavo si (of selma'o SI) is a metalinguistic operator that erases the preceding word, as if it had never been spoken:
means the same thing as ti mlatu. Multiple si cmavo in succession erase the appropriate number of words:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: ta blanu zdani si si xekri zdani
interlinear-gloss.gloss: That is-a-blue house, er, er, is-a-black house.

section.para:
erasureof quotations with "zo"
For erasure purposes, a construct that the word-level machinery has bound into a single unit – a zo quotation, a lo'u…le'u quotation, a zoi quotation, a zei compound, or a word with bu – counts as one word: zo .bab. si erases the whole quotation, not just .bab.. One consequence is that a zo spoken in error cannot be erased directly, because zo quotes whatever follows it – including a si. The way out is to let it do so, and then erase the resulting quotation:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: zo .bab. se cmene zo si si la .bab.
interlinear-gloss.gloss: The-word Bob is-the-name-of the-word- si , er, Bob.

section.para: The first si does not erase anything: it is captured by zo , forming the quotation zo si (the word si). The second si then erases that quotation as a single unit. (The first edition, which counted the pieces of a quotation as separate words for erasure, required three; texts and tools from that era may reflect the old accounting.)
Incorrect names can likewise cause trouble with si :

The Lojbanized spelling .esperanto breaks up, as a consequence of the Lojban morphology rules (see ) into two Lojban words, the cmavo .e and the undefined lujvo speranto. Therefore, two si cmavo are needed to erase them. Of course, .e speranto is not grammatical after la , but recognition of si is done before grammatical analysis.

erasurequotes
Even more messy is the result of an incorrect zoi :

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi cusku zoi fy. gy. .fy. si zo .djan.

section.para:
In
, the first fy. is taken to be the delimiting word. The quoted material runs until the next occurrence of that same word, so the delimiting word itself cannot appear inside the payload; gy. , the Lojban name for the letter g , was chosen arbitrarily as the (one-word) payload here – even an empty payload would do. Then the delimiting word is repeated, closing the quotation – and the whole quotation, delimiters and all, is now a single word as far as si is concerned, so one si erases it. Similarly, a stray lo'u quotation mark is repaired by completing the quotation and erasing it as a unit: fy. le'u si.
There is no way to erase less than an entire quotation: si sees the bound construct, not its parts. To replace the word quoted by zo , erase the whole quotation and start over:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi se cmene zo .djan. si zo .djordj.
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I - am-named-by the-word John, er, the-word George.

section.para: A parser will reject mi se cmene zo .djan. si si .djordj. -style attempts to peel the quotation apart: the first si removes the quotation whole, the second then eats cmene – there is no leftover half-quotation for it to trim – and the sentence collapses.

Modern Lojban parsers implement si erasure exactly as described here. (The first edition's note that the current machine parser does not implement si erasure described the software of its day and is long obsolete.)

erasuremultiple word
precise erasures starting marker As the above examples plainly show, precise erasures with si can be extremely hard to get right. Therefore, the cmavo sa (of selma'o SA) is provided for erasing more than one word. The cmavo following sa should be the starting marker of some grammatical construct. The effect of the sa is to erase back to and including the last starting marker of the same kind. For example:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi viska le sa .i mi cusku zo .djan.
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I see the ... - I say the-word John.

section.para:
Since the word following sa is .i , the sentence separator, its effect is to erase the preceding sentence. So
is equivalent to:
Another example, erasing a partial description rather than a partial sentence:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi viska le blanu .zdan. sa le xekri zdani
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I see the blue hou ... the black house.

section.para:
In
, le blanu .zdan. is ungrammatical, but clearly reflects the speaker's original intention to say le blanu zdani. However, the zdani was cut off before the end and changed into a cmevla. The entire ungrammatical le construct is erased and replaced by le xekri zdani.

saunsettled status of
A frank status note: sa is the least settled word in this section. The description above – erase back to the last construct of the same kind as what follows – conveys the intent, and simple uses like the examples are understood by everyone. But the precise rule was deliberately left undecided when the rest of the word-level machinery was standardized, a later community proposal (erase back to the last word of the same selma'o) never gained official standing, and today's parsers implement differing approximations: of the two examples above, one current parser accepts both, another accepts only the second. Use sa freely in speech, where a human listener does the repair work; in text meant for machines, prefer si or rephrasing, and do not build clever constructions on sa's exotic corners.

erasuretotal
multiple speakers The cmavo su (of selma'o SU) is yet another metalinguistic operator that erases everything said so far – more precisely, back to the nearest preceding structural boundary: the beginning of the text, or a paragraph break with ni'o , or the opening of a quotation with lu , of a tu'e…tu'u group, or of a to…toi parenthesis. Erasing back to such a boundary rather than blindly to the start of everything keeps su usable inside quotations and parentheses. By convention, in a conversation su abandons only the speaker's own remarks; susu abandons the whole discussion.

sustatus of
(A status note: like si , su was deliberately left out of the committee's 2005 decisions, so the boundary rule above is de facto – it comes from the community's erasure proposal and is unvoted. Implementation is also uneven at present: the standard camxes grammar erases back to the boundary and preserves it, as described, while at least one other current parser mishandles the boundary itself; erasing from the start of a text works everywhere.)

section.title: Hesitation: Y
section.para: The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

Speakers often need to hesitate to think of what to say next or for some extra-linguistic reason. There are two ways to hesitate in Lojban: to pause between words (that is, to say nothing) or to use the cmavo .y. (of selma'o Y). This resembles in sound the English hesitation noise written uh (or er), but differs from it in the requirement for pauses before and after. Unlike a long pause, it cannot be mistaken for having nothing more to say: it holds the floor for the speaker. Since vowel length is not significant in Lojban, the y sound can be dragged out for as long as necessary. Furthermore, the sound can be repeated, provided the required pauses are respected.

hesitation sound Since the hesitation sound in English is outside the formal language, English-speakers may question the need for a formal cmavo. Speakers of other languages, however, often hesitate by saying (or, if necessary, repeating) a word ( este in some dialects of Spanish, roughly meaning that is), and Lojban's audio-visual isomorphism requires a written representation of all meaningful spoken behavior. Of course, .y. has no grammatical significance: it can appear anywhere at all in a Lojban sentence except in the middle of a word. Even the word-level machinery of this chapter treats it as if it were silence: a hesitation between, say, a word and an erasing si changes nothing. The single exception is the letteral .ybu (the name of the letter y), which is recognized as a unit before anything else happens; see .

yword-level invisibility, status
(A status note: the invisibility of .y. to the word-level machinery, and the .ybu exception, are checkpointed rules: the committee's frozen 2005 definition of the hesitation sound states both, down to the consequence that zo cannot quote .y..)

section.title: No more to say: FAhO
section.para: The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

yielding the floor end of file computer interaction unconditional signal The cmavo fa'o (of selma'o FAhO) is the usually omitted marker for the end of a text; it can be used in computer interaction to indicate the end of input or output, or for explicitly giving up the floor during a discussion. It is outside the regular grammar: once an effective fa'o is reached, nothing after it is read at all. A fa'o is ineffective only if some earlier word-level operator has already captured it – quoted with zo , inside lo'u ... le'u , serving as the delimiter of a zoi quotation or lying inside its payload, or bound into a compound with zei. In particular, it is not used at the end of subordinate texts quoted with lu … li'u or parenthesized with to ... toi.

fa'ostatus of
(A status note: the fa'o rule and its capture exceptions are checkpointed. The committee's frozen 2005 text-structure definition names capture by zo , by lo'u…le'u , by use as a zoi delimiter, and by a preceding zei ; capture inside a zoi payload follows from the separately checkpointed zoi rule of the quotations decision.)

section.title: How the magic words interact
section.para: magic words left-to-right rule The words discussed in this chapter that operate on words as words – zo , zoi and la'o , lo'u (with its delimiter le'u), zei , bu , si , sa , su , and fa'o – are informally called the magic words. They act before the ordinary grammar sees the text, and the first edition specified their interactions with a list of pairwise exceptions that was neither complete nor entirely consistent. This edition replaces that list with one uniform principle:

para.emphasis: Magic words take effect strictly left to right. Whatever an earlier magic word has captured is no longer available to a later one; the product of a quotation or compound acts as a single word for the machinery that follows.

section.para: Two small preliminaries complete the picture: the letteral .ybu is recognized as a single word before anything else happens, and the hesitation sound .y. is invisible to this machinery altogether ().
Everything the first edition's list said, insofar as it was right, follows from the principle. A few worked consequences:

listitem.para: zo si is a quotation of si , not an erasure: zo comes first and captures the si. The same holds for zo zo , zo fa'o , and indeed zo before any word at all ( .y. excepted, as always).
Inside a lo'u…le'u or zoi quotation, nothing operates: the quotation opened first, so everything up to its closing word is mere quoted material. A si or fa'o in there erases and terminates nothing.

A completed quotation or zei compound is one word thereafter: one si erases all of zo .bab. or broda zei brode ; bu after zo .bab. makes a letteral out of the quoted word; an attitudinal after it comments on the whole of it.

zei joins the single word (or already-formed unit) on each side of it into one brivla; bu binds the single word or unit before it into a letteral, and may be repeated. Neither can reach past a magic word that acted earlier, and a bu or zei with nothing available to bind is simply ungrammatical.

ba'e marks the next word, and attitudinals of UI and CAI (with an attached nai , if any) comment on the previous word or unit; but neither fuses with its target – a later magic word still sees them as separate words. Thus broda ba'e da si da erases only the da , leaving the emphasis marker to claim the replacement.

section.para:
magic wordsstatus of interaction rules
Status: the single uniform principle stated above is this edition's synthesis, following the community's later unification of these rules and the behavior of current parsers – it was never voted as such. What the language-definition committee actually fixed, word by word, in its 2005 checkpoints is the left-to-right conflict rule for each of the quoting and binding words individually: for lo'u , zo , zoi , and la'o in its quotations decision, for zei in its connectives decision, and for bu by a definition that used an exception list rather than the uniform principle. The y and fa'o rules have their own checkpointed definitions. The erasure words were deliberately left out of those decisions: si and su as taught here are de facto (implemented but unvoted), and sa remains unsettled (). Wherever the checkpointed per-word rules and the uniform principle agree – which is almost everywhere – the principle simply restates settled material; one corner is genuinely contested: whether bu may bind a preceding ba'e (making a ba'e letteral) – the checkpointed bu text forbade it, while the uniform principle and current parsers allow it. Treat ba'e bu and similar exotica as curiosities, not tools. One more limit of the single word metaphor: under the later (unvoted) selma'o-matching proposal for sa , a quotation still remembers the selma'o of the word that formed it – the frozen quotation definitions preserve ZO for a zo quote, ZOI for zoi and la'o , and LOhU and LEhU for the two ends of a lo'u…le'u quote, precisely so that such matching can work.

section.title: List of elidable terminators
section.para: The following list shows all the elidable terminators of Lojban. The first column is the terminator, the second column is the selma'o that starts the corresponding construction, and the third column states what kinds of grammatical constructs are terminated. Each terminator is the only cmavo of its selma'o, which naturally has the same name as the cmavo.

cmavo-entry.description: sumti attached to a tanru unit
